one_liner: Telegram supports bot-scoped messaging, but a bot token does not grant access to a user’s personal inbox or full chat history.

auth.notes: An MTProto user-authorized session lets an integration call the Telegram API as the user. The app’s api_id and api_hash are required for authorization but do not sign the user in. A BotFather token authenticates the bot, not the user. A separately authorized business connection lets a bot handle updates and send messages on the user’s behalf within its permissions. Telegram Gateway accepts a bearer token for verification-code delivery. Telegram Login uses OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with OpenID Connect for sign-in; its optional telegram:bot_access scope lets the linked bot send direct messages to the user, not read their chats.

access.notes: Register a free bot through @BotFather to obtain a token for the hosted Bot API. Standard messaging is free within rate limits, with optional paid broadcasts for higher volume. MTProto requires an active Telegram account and app registration at my.telegram.org. Running the Bot API server locally replaces the API endpoint, not Telegram’s hosted messaging service.

api.notes: The Bot API uses method-oriented HTTPS/JSON endpoints to send and edit messages, forward media, look up chats, and receive updates by webhook or polling. Bots ordinarily cannot start private conversations, see only relevant group messages by default, and cannot retrieve full chat history from the update queue. MTProto provides broader user-client access, including message history and contacts.

mcp.notes: No Telegram-published MCP server was found. The community package @iqai/mcp-telegram uses a BotFather token and supports sending, forwarding, pinning, and chat lookup. Composio advertises a separate managed MCP option.

verdict.rationale: Free, self-serve credentials and a documented API make bot-scoped messaging practical, but a bot token does not grant access to a user’s personal inbox or full chat history. Before using Telegram conversations in an agent, review Telegram’s content-licensing terms, which restrict AI use of platform data and describe possible exceptions based on ongoing, context-specific consent from all relevant users.

verification.note: The quotes support bot tokens, user-authorized sessions, bearer tokens for Gateway, and an authorization-code login flow. They do not establish every detail in the notes, such as the named bot-access scope.

Telegram says the Bot Platform is free for developers and that messaging BotFather yields an authentication token. The quotes do not establish the notes' details about MTProto registration or optional paid broadcasts.

The quotes establish a public HTTP Bot API and a separate API for custom clients; they do not contradict the estimated breadth. Several specific capabilities in the notes, including editing messages and retrieving contacts, are not shown.
The GitHub quote describes a functioning third-party server. It does not substantiate the notes' claims about the named package's specific features or a separate managed MCP option.
The quote comes from Composio's Telegram toolkit page and describes its integration.

Free self-serve bot credentials and a documented, useful API support buildability. The evidenced bot limitations support a caveat and an 'other' blocker; the cited licensing restriction also supports the rationale.
